title: Shia theology
hook: roots and branches: how Twelver Shia teaching sets out the beliefs that hold everything up

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Athari approach, and your line: as it came. Did you repeat something back exactly before explaining it? Today, Shia theology, and its own map of belief. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

A tree has branches you can see: leaves, fruit, the shade you sit in. And it has roots you can't see, holding the whole thing up. Twelver Shia teaching uses exactly that picture. Prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, charity: those are furu' al-din, the branches of religion. The beliefs underneath are usul al-din, the roots. And one detail in it stands out. In the branches, Twelver Shia Muslims follow a qualified scholar's rulings. In the roots, the teaching goes, each person should hold the beliefs through their own understanding, not just because someone said so. Today, the roots.
screen: `BRANCHES YOU CAN SEE.` → `ROOTS YOU CAN'T.` → `HOLD THE ROOTS YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Twelver Shia theology names the roots as tawhid, the oneness of Allah; 'adl, His justice; nubuwwa, prophethood; imama, the imamate; and ma'ad, the return, the resurrection and the Last Day. Oneness, prophethood and the return appear in Sunni creeds too. Two stand out, and they're the two words in today's line. Justice first. Justice sits in the roots here. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness." Shia theologians hold that Allah does nothing unjust and nothing without wisdom, and that He never asks of anyone what they can't do. On this point Shia theology stands close to the Mu'tazilah we met a few days ago, and the two traditions shared arguments. Then guidance. Shia teaching holds that Allah does not leave people without a guide. After the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, guidance continues through imams from his household, beginning with Ali, divinely chosen and protected from error. In Twelver belief the twelfth imam is alive and hidden, in what's called the occultation, and will return. There's a hadith both Sunnis and Shia know. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people, the Book of Allah and the people of his household. Shia scholars read it as pointing to the imams. Sunni teaching also honors the Prophet's household, but they don't count the imamate among the roots of faith. Zaydi and Isma'ili Shia have their own accounts too. Justice and guidance, in this teaching: a God who is fair, and who does not leave people without a guide.
screen: `USUL: THE ROOTS OF RELIGION.` · `'ADL: ALLAH DOES NOTHING UNJUST.` · `IMAMA: GUIDANCE CONTINUES.` · then, large: `TWO WEIGHTY THINGS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the roots. Settle, and breathe. Picture a tree, and let its roots go down one at a time as you name them. Tawhid: oneness. 'Adl: justice. Nubuwwa: prophethood. Imama: guidance through the imams. Ma'ad: the return. Then go through them again, slower, with just the Arabic words. Don't worry about getting them perfect. Notice which root you'd most like to understand better, and stay with that one. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Shia theology. In Twelver teaching, the roots of religion: oneness, justice, prophethood, the imamate, and the return. Today's word.

Your line: justice and guidance. Today, be fair to one person who doesn't expect it, and point one person toward something good. Tomorrow, free will and decree. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims learn the usul al-din, the roots of religion (tawhid, 'adl, nubuwwa, imama and ma'ad), and are taught to hold them through their own understanding, while following a qualified scholar in matters of practice.
